title: Make JsonSerializerOptionsExtensions public
body:
# Pull Request

## Description of Changes
The `JsonSerializerOptionsExtensions` class is currently marked internal, which means the `AspNetCoreSseServer` sample code won't work elsewhere.
E.g. grabbing `McpEndpointRouteBuilderExtensions` and putting it in a new project and referencing `mcpdotnet` causes a compile error because of the following line (amongst others):
```csharp
var message = await context.Request.ReadFromJsonAsync<IJsonRpcMessage>(JsonSerializerOptionsExtensions.DefaultOptions, context.RequestAborted);
```
Making it public resolves the compile error, and the server works quite nicely.

Apologies in advance if I've missed something obvious. If that's the case, feel free to close out the PR.                

## Related Issue(s)
I did not create an issue for this item.

## Testing Done
- [ ] Unit tests added/updated
- [ ] Integration tests added/updated
- [x] Manual testing performed

## Breaking Changes
None

comments.body: cc: @halter73, @eiriktsarpalis
AspNetCoreSseServer Not only as a demo, but can it be considered to be encapsulated into a library?

Open to whatever the maintainers feel best though.

The long term plan is to move SseServerStreamTransport or something like it into the core library, so it won’t be necessary to make JsonSerializerOptionsExtensions.DefaultOptions public for the ASP.NET Core sample to work.

That said, I could still see it being useful to make the options public, but I’d move it to a class and rename it.

I think forking and patching the implementation is reasonable if you need something working right now. I'll try to ensure we either move SseServerStreamTransport into the core library or expose the default JsonSerializerOptions publically before we cut the next release.

title: Review library for protocol completeness
body:
We should conduct a review checking that all facets of the MCP specification are being implemented by this library.

## Known issues

- [ ] Logging is not implemented. It's an optional utility capability (server to client). Configuration should be added on the client side to easily integrate with logging. Very few users will want to actually implement a client-side handler for this. Server side configuration could also be added to integrate directly with a logger. I am not sure the protocol model matches logging extensions, so might need to make the mapping configurable (nice-to-have).
- [ ] Authorization (also optional) is also not implemented, but I am not sure any MCP SDK implements that fully according to spec, and most don't at all.
- [ ] There are also some request / response schemas which support free-form _meta / additional properties patterns not implemented. Some of these are not particularly pleasant outside weakly typed languages, so in the local branch where I'm doing such a completeness pass I'm considering just using JsonElement for them. Not sure what the best way to support these is - will find some examples later.
- [ ] Notification capability flags are not enforced server side. Servers must not send notifications to clients that are not declared in capabilities. This is currently possible to do as a server author.
author: eiriktsarpalis

comments.body:
Logging is not implemented. It's an optional utility capability (server to client). Authorization (also optional) is also not implemented, but I am not sure any MCP SDK implements that fully according to spec, and most don't at all.

There are also some request / response schemas which support free-form _meta / additional properties patterns not implemented. Some of these are not particularly pleasant outside weakly typed languages, so in the local branch where I'm doing such a completeness pass I'm considering just using JsonElement for them. Not sure what the best way to support these is - will find some examples later.
Thanks Peder, I've transcribed your points into checkboxes in my OP. Feel free to edit my post to modify/append as appropriate.
Added additional comments about logging to the OP.
Is support for subscring to and unsubscribing from resources implemented? I see the delegates, but I'm not clear on when those are invoked.

> Is support for subscring to and unsubscribing from resources implemented? I see the delegates, but I'm not clear on when those are invoked.

It is supported on a protocol level, but implementing the logic is currently up to the user. I think a convenience programming model which encapsulates a resource collection and wraps the list / get logic of that capability could also handle this on the server side.

So I'd say in terms of protocol completeness: yes - but in terms of library/SDK completeness: no.

(And I realize that what I call convenience is what many, if not most, others consider core SDK functionality. But the raw MCP implementation is there, so a library user could handle these whether client or server, with the current support. They'd just be on their own, but that's also the case for implementing list / get. But I do agree that such functionality should be added, but that it should also be possible to hook directly into the protocol and provide a custom implementation if one wants to do that.)

> It is supported on a protocol level

I'm missing even that part. McpServer has the delegates, but what invokes then? Are they supposed to be hooked up to some incoming notification/request?

> > It is supported on a protocol level
> 
> I'm missing even that part. McpServer has the delegates, but what invokes then? Are they supposed to be hooked up to some incoming notification/request?

I'll add integration tests. If I missed something, I'll find out, and add it. But I think it should be there - it's just a handler, there's no logic - nothing on the server which invokes, as the subscription is initiated by the client. 

It's up to the implementation of the server (ie library user) to store the subscriptions and to send notification events. Likewise, it's up to the client when to create subscriptions and how to handle notification events.

This is where the resource wrapper will be handy. The vast majority of users would just want a collection of resources and to have built-in subscription, list, list change and get functionality, and not provide custom handlers.

Yeah, there's a bug in the SubcribeToResources and UnsubscribeToResources implementation. I am fixing it now. The types are not right. I'll have a PR with a fix before long.

Edit: #89 fixes the issues (there was also a handler registration issue).

title: Remove InputOutputStreams and clean up StdioServerTransport ctors
body:
- There doesn't appear to be a meaningful scenario for injecting different readers/writers than stdin/stdout, and having InputOutputStreams complicates the API.
- Logically folks talk about "input and output", "readers and writers", etc., and "stdio" is "standard input and output", so having input specified first is less likely to be a source of bugs.
- Logger should be optional, not required, to simplify the common and getting-started cases.

What are the scenarios for configuring the std input / output with the server? What else would someone reasonably supply? And if it's important for the server, is it also important for the client such that we should similarly be enabling it there?
author: stephentoub

comments.body:
I agree. I might have gotten a bit overwhelmed with the volume of contributions and missed this additional complexity being added in one of them. I don't think it should be added until proven to be needed in an actual production scenario (with no reasonable alternative).

Also agree on the logger. My intent with having it in the constructor was to make use of no logging an explicit choice, and not an oversight. I am happy to defer to your experience and insight on the best patterns for that kind of "encouragement".

> My intent with having it in the constructor was to make use of no logging an explicit choice, and not an oversight

Perfectly fair. The concern is just that a lot of systems configure the default logger to be for the console, which obviously is problematic here. If someones starting out with the APIs, they also are very likely to either provide a null logger if they're forced to provide one, or a console logger.

I think for now we don't require it. We can (and should) revisit all of this, though, holistically for the entire API surface area at some point in the near future.

title: Improved Mechanism for Propagating Tool Failure
body:
Tool failure (using IsError = true) is currently not possible to return from the Tool mapping layer. This could be done via:

1) Enforcing all Tools return a ToolResult type which has an IsError field. This is not desirable as it removes the ability to expose any method as tool.

2) A new Exception (ie McpToolException) which is caught in the handler and then returns IsError true and an error message provided in the exception. This would allow developers a way to hook into the MCP protocol without enforcing specific return types on their method.
author: PederHP

comments.body: I assume any exception would be mapped to IsError=true, possibly with special-casing if there are error codes that map to specific exception types, like cancellation, and then a custom mcp exception type could also be special-cased if it carries an exact error code?
